name: Corner Blend
producer: Sítio Bela Vista and twelve smallholders in Huila
notes: Milk chocolate, toasted hazelnut, dried fig
description: The one in the hopper every day. Built to hold its shape through a flat white without losing the fruit underneath.
content:
Corner Blend is the only coffee we have never taken off the bar. It is two thirds Yellow Catuaí from Sítio Bela Vista in the Mantiqueira hills — pulped natural, dried on raised beds, and relentlessly sweet — cut with a washed Caturra lot from a group of twelve smallholders around Pitalito.

The Brazilian half gives the shot its body and the long chocolate finish. The Colombian half keeps it from going flat: a red-apple acidity that survives whole milk, which is the whole reason the blend exists. We adjust the ratio twice a year as the harvests turn over, always tasting for the same thing — a flat white that still tastes like fruit at the bottom of the cup.

How we pull it

18g in, 40g out, 27 to 30 seconds, 93°C. If it runs fast it turns sharp; if it runs slow the hazelnut turns to ash. It is forgiving in the middle and unforgiving at the edges, which makes it a good coffee to learn on.

name: Aricha
description: The one people come back for. Dried on the bed for eighteen days and it tastes like it — jammy, floral, faintly wild.
content:
Aricha is a washing station, not a farm — around 340 smallholders in the hills above Yirgacheffe deliver cherry here through the harvest, most of them working plots smaller than a tennis court. What comes out the other end is the coffee most people mean when they say they like Ethiopian coffee.

This is the natural lot: whole cherry laid on raised beds for eighteen days, turned by hand through the heat of the day. Done badly that gets you something boozy and flat. Done at this altitude, with this much fuss, you get blueberry and jasmine and a black-tea finish that lasts a genuinely long time.

Brewing it

Go coarser than you think and keep the water hot. It is a forgiving coffee at 15g to 250g, and it will still taste like itself if you leave it to go cold — which, for what it's worth, is our favourite way to drink it.

name: Kirundo
description: Clean, bright and structured. The coffee we hand to people who say they don't like fruity coffee.
content:
Nkonge Hill sits at 1,750 metres in Kayanza, close enough to the Rwandan border that the coffee shares a family resemblance with the lots across it. Red Bourbon, fully washed, fermented under water overnight and then dried slowly on beds under shade cloth.

Washed Burundis at this altitude do something we have never quite been able to talk customers into in advance: they taste bright without tasting sour. Redcurrant up front, brown sugar through the middle, and a twist of orange peel right at the end. It is structured in a way naturals rarely are.

On the bar

This is our batch brew most of the winter — 60g per litre, five and a half minutes. It holds beautifully in the urn for an hour, which is not something you can say about most light roasts.

name: La Serranía
description: Eleven hectares in Acevedo, run by two people. Pink Bourbon picked in three passes and fermented longer than anyone else on the ridge.
content:
Óscar and Marta Peña farm eleven hectares on a ridge above Acevedo, and they have been growing Pink Bourbon there since well before anyone was paying a premium for it. They pick in three passes rather than stripping the branch, which costs them time and gets them a lot with almost no underripes in it.

The fermentation is the other half of the story: 36 hours in sealed tanks, roughly twice as long as their neighbours, before washing and drying on a covered patio. It builds a syrupy sweetness into a washed coffee that would otherwise read as simply clean.

What to expect

Peach, unmistakably — the kind that is just soft enough to eat. Then demerara sugar, then a dry almond finish that keeps the whole thing from being cloying. It is the coffee we put on when we want to show someone what washed Colombian coffee can be.

name: Gatare
description: A honey process from Nyamasheke that lands somewhere between the washed and natural camps. On the bar until the sacks run out.
content:
Gatare sits above Lake Kivu in Nyamasheke, and the station has been experimenting with honey processing for a few seasons now — pulping the cherry but leaving the mucilage on through drying, so the bean takes on some of the fruit without the ferment of a full natural.

The result splits the difference in a way we find genuinely useful. There is rhubarb sharpness from the washed side and cocoa-nib depth from the natural side, tied together with plain cane sugar. It brews well hot and it is exceptional over ice.

Seasonal, and we mean it

We buy Gatare one pallet at a time and we do not reorder. When the sacks are gone the space on the shelf goes to whatever landed next — which is the honest way to sell a coffee this dependent on one particular drying season.
